questions.stem: Working the problem, how many chlorine atoms are present in thionyl chloride, SOCl2?

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count nitrogen atoms in the products
questions.stem: Working the problem, hydrolysis of one mole of acetamide produces one mole of ammonia-derived amine. How many nitrogen atoms are in that amine product?
questions.explanation: Acetamide contains one nitrogen atom, and basic hydrolysis transfers it into one molecule of ammonia or amine, so the nitrogen is conserved as a single atom in the product.
questions.hint: Nitrogen is conserved one to one.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why are acid chlorides more reactive than amides toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?

answer.exemplar: Chloride is a good leaving group and strongly withdraws electron density, making the carbonyl very electrophilic; in an amide the nitrogen donates its lone pair by resonance, decreasing electrophilicity, and the amide anion would be a terrible leaving group, so amides are far less reactive.

questions.explanation: Leaving-group ability and resonance donation set the order. Chloride is a good leaving group and strongly withdraws electron density, making the carbonyl very electrophilic; in an amide the nitrogen donates its lone pair by resonance, decreasing electrophilicity, and the amide anion would be a terrible leaving group, so amides are far less reactive.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why does removing water increase ester yield?

answer.exemplar: Esterification is an equilibrium, and water is a product; continuously removing water lowers its concentration and, by Le Chatelier's principle, shifts the equilibrium toward forming more ester and water until a new balance is reached.

questions.explanation: Removing a product drives the reaction forward. questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why is base-promoted ester hydrolysis effectively irreversible while acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is reversible?

answer.exemplar: Base hydrolysis produces a carboxylate anion that is resonance stabilized and not electrophilic, so the alcohol cannot attack it to regenerate ester; in acid the carboxylic acid product remains electrophilic and can re-esterify, giving a true equilibrium.

questions.explanation: Carboxylate cannot be attacked back. Base hydrolysis produces a carboxylate anion that is resonance stabilized and not electrophilic, so the alcohol cannot attack it to regenerate ester; in acid the carboxylic acid product remains electrophilic and can re-esterify, giving a true equilibrium.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why does nitrile hydrolysis pass through an amide intermediate?

answer.exemplar: Water adds to the carbon-nitrogen triple bond to give an imidic acid that tautomerizes to an amide, and continued hydrolysis of the amide under the same conditions then gives the carboxylic acid; the amide is therefore an obligatory intermediate on the route to the acid.

questions.explanation: Hydration gives an amide before the acid. Water adds to the carbon-nitrogen triple bond to give an imidic acid that tautomerizes to an amide, and continued hydrolysis of the amide under the same conditions then gives the carboxylic acid; the amide is therefore an obligatory intermediate on the route to the acid.

questions.explanation: Friedel-Crafts reactions require an electron-rich enough ring to attack the carbocation-like electrophile; strongly deactivated rings such as nitrobenzene do not react, and aniline also fails because it complexes with the Lewis acid.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a practice exercise, what is the active electrophile in aromatic nitration using nitric and sulfuric acids?
questions.explanation: Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which loses water to give the linear nitronium ion, a powerful electrophile that the aromatic ring attacks to form a sigma complex.
questions.hint: Nitronium ion is the nitrating electrophile.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a practice exercise, which Lewis acid is commonly used for Friedel-Crafts acylation with an acid chloride?

options.misconception: sodium chloride is not a Lewis acid catalyst
that is used in other contexts, not standard here

questions.explanation: Aluminum chloride coordinates to the acid chloride, generating an acylium ion electrophile that the aromatic ring attacks; the resulting ketone complexes with the Lewis acid and is released on aqueous workup.
questions.hint: Aluminum chloride generates the acylium ion.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a practice exercise, what distinguishes aromatic sulfonation from nitration and halogenation?

options.text: Sulfonation is reversible on heating with dilute acid
Sulfonation does not use an electrophile

options.misconception: the sulfo group is meta directing but position depends on existing groups

questions.explanation: Sulfonation is reversible, so it can be used as a temporary blocking group: the sulfonic acid can be removed by heating with dilute acid, unlike nitration or halogenation which are essentially irreversible.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a practice exercise, what is the key intermediate in electrophilic aromatic substitution?

options.misconception: a phenyl cation is not formed
the process is cationic, not radical

questions.explanation: Attack of the electrophile gives a cyclohexadienyl cation called the sigma complex or arenium ion, whose positive charge is delocalized over the ring before loss of a proton restores aromaticity.
questions.hint: Arenium ion is the sigma complex.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a practice exercise, a ring bearing both a methyl group and a nitro group undergoes nitration. Which group mainly controls the position of the new substituent?
questions.explanation: When activating and deactivating groups conflict, the stronger activating group controls orientation, so a methyl group directs the incoming electrophile ortho or para even in the presence of a nitro group.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a practice exercise, which catalyst is needed to chlorinate benzene with chlorine gas?

options.misconception: sodium is not a Lewis acid catalyst
that is used for halide precipitation

questions.explanation: Iron(III) chloride, often generated in situ from iron and chlorine, polarizes the chlorine molecule to generate a strong electrophile that benzene can attack in electrophilic aromatic substitution.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a practice exercise, which reagent converts an aryl diazonium salt into an aryl chloride?

options.misconception: chloride alone will not replace diazonium
that is insoluble and unreactive here

questions.explanation: The Sandmeyer reaction uses copper(I) chloride to replace the diazonium group with chlorine, proceeding through an aryl radical and copper-mediated chlorine transfer.
